title: The second boon given; the third asked for
theme: Yama closes the second boon — this is your fire to heaven, and people will call it by your name — and invites the third.

sandhi.type: eṣaḥ before a consonant; e before a
sandhi.rule: eṣaḥ loses its visarga before a consonant, P. 6.1.132 (एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि); e before a absorbs it (shown by the avagraha), P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति); the visarga after i becomes r.

sandhi.type: visarga before a voiced consonant; m before a vowel
sandhi.rule: aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes o: P. 6.1.114 (हशि च) with P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः); m stays before a vowel.
Visarga before t becomes s: P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः).
aḥ before a voiced consonant becomes o: P. 6.1.114 (हशि च).

morphology.note: Vedic nominative plural in -āsaḥ (= janāḥ), formed with the augment asuk: P. 7.1.50 (आज्जसेरसुक्).
Imperfect middle 2 sg. of vṛ ‘choose’ (ninth class).
Enclitic dative or genitive of tvam; Śaṅkara takes it as dative, ‘for you’.

translation.literal: ‘This is your fire, O Naciketas, leading to heaven, which you chose with the second boon. People will call this fire yours indeed. Choose the third boon, O Naciketas.’
translation.readable: ‘This, Naciketas, is the fire that leads to heaven, the one you chose as your second gift. People will call it by your name. Now, Naciketas, choose your third gift.’

syntax: Three sentences: a summary of the second boon with a relative clause (yam avṛṇīthā dvitīyena vareṇa), a statement about the future name of the fire, and the invitation tṛtīyaṃ varaṃ naciketo vṛṇīṣva. The vocative naciketaḥ frames the speech.

ambiguities.note: Madhva’s text reads nāciketaḥ, ‘the Nāciketa [fire]’, an adjective of agniḥ, for the vocative naciketaḥ (corrections.json).

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: Counted as written, 22 and 26 syllables: the second line (etam agniṃ tavaiva pravakṣyanti janāsas tṛtīyaṃ varaṃ naciketo vṛṇīṣva) is four syllables long; janāsaḥ and the extra vocative may have been read with contractions, or the line is irregular.

beginner: Yama closes the second gift and opens the way to the third. This, he says, is the fire that leads to heaven, the one you chose; and people will call it by your name. Now choose your third gift. Śaṅkara adds a touching detail: Yama feels he owes the boy until the third boon is given, as one feels in debt to an honoured guest. The scene is set for the most important question of the Upaniṣad, which Naciketas will ask in the next verse. Everything so far has been preparation for it.
analogy: Like a host who has served two courses and now, before the last one, asks the guest what he would most like.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The second boon, the fire to heaven, is given and will bear Naciketas’s name among people; now he must choose the third.

commentary.q: Why must the third be given?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: Yama counts the naming as a fourth boon given from pleasure, «एष वरो दत्तो मया चतुर्थस्तुष्टेन», and feels himself in debt until the third is given: «तस्मिन्ह्यदत्ते ऋणवानेवाहमित्यभिप्रायः».

commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: He uses this point for a long argument that ‘heaven’ in the second boon means release, reporting the Śrībhāṣya: «स्वर्गशब्देनात्र परमपुरुषार्थलक्षणमोक्षोऽभिधीयते», because those who reach it are said to have immortality and to cross birth and death, and because a boy who scorns perishable fruits would not ask for a perishable heaven. He then states the objections and answers them.

advaita.text: The ritual section ends; the boons so far concern action and its fruits. Yama feels indebted until the third is given: «तस्मिन्ह्यदत्ते ऋणवानेवाहमित्यभिप्रायः».

visistadvaita.text: Heaven throughout the second boon is release: «स्वर्गशब्देनात्र परमपुरुषार्थलक्षणमोक्षोऽभिधीयते». He also reads the people’s naming plainly: «जनाः तवैव नाम्ना एनमग्निं प्रवक्ष्यन्ति इत्यर्थः».

dvaita.text: Madhva has no separate comment on this verse; the verse he cites from the Pādma states the naming of the fire: «यमोऽनुवादसन्तुष्टो वह्नेस्तन्नामतामपि». His text reads nāciketaḥ, the name of the fire.

schools.disagreement: The verse itself is a hinge; the schools differ on what has just been given. Śaṅkara: a ritual leading to a high heaven. Raṅgarāmānuja: a means of release. Madhva: the fire in which Hari is present (1.1.12–13).

contemporary.text: Naciketas has waited through two boons — family peace and a ritual — before the question that matters most to him. People often need to settle smaller things before they can ask the large one. (A modern reflection.)

reflect.beginner: What question would you keep for last, if you were given three?
reflect.deeper: Why might the Upaniṣad make us wait for the main question?
reflect.practice: Write down the question about your life that you most want answered, and leave it there for a day.

flags.note: Madhva’s text reads nāciketaḥ (the fire’s name) for the vocative naciketaḥ (corrections.json).
